Once, though, the lieutenant asked why he had travelled so far across the ice in such an unusual vehicle.

His face immediately darkened with the deepest sorrow. “To find someone who ran away from me,” he answered.

“And was the man you were following travelling in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I believe we saw him. The day before we rescued you, we saw dogs pulling a sledge across the ice with a man riding in it.”

The stranger became alert at this news. He asked many questions about the route taken by the person he called the demon. Soon afterward, when we were alone, he said, “I must have stirred your curiosity, as well as that of these kind people. But you are too thoughtful to question me.”

“Of course. It would be both rude and cruel to trouble you simply to satisfy my curiosity.”

“And yet you saved me from a strange and dangerous situation. Through your kindness, you have brought me back to life.”

A little later, he asked whether I thought the breaking ice had destroyed the other sledge. I told him I could not say with any certainty. The ice had not broken up until nearly midnight, and the traveller might have reached safety by then. But I had no way of knowing.

From that moment, fresh energy seemed to fill the stranger’s weakened body. He was extremely eager to go on deck and look for the sledge we had seen before. I have persuaded him to stay in the cabin, however, because he is much too weak to bear the cold, damp air. I promised that someone would keep watch for him and tell him immediately if anything new appeared in the distance.

This is my account of everything connected with this strange event up to today. The stranger’s health has gradually improved, but he speaks very little and seems uncomfortable whenever anyone but me enters his cabin. Still, his manner is so gentle and pleasant that all the sailors care about him, even though they have scarcely spoken to him. I am beginning to love him like a brother. His deep, unending sorrow fills me with sympathy and pity. He must have been an exceptional man in happier days, since even in his ruined state he remains so appealing and kind.

In one of my letters, dear Margaret, I said that I would find no friend on this vast ocean. Yet I have found a man whom I would gladly have welcomed as a brother of my heart, before suffering broke his spirit.

Just as they left the dining room, the tower clock began to strike midnight. With the final stroke came a crash and a sudden, piercing cry. A terrible clap of thunder shook the house, and strange, unearthly music drifted through the air. At the top of the stairs, a panel burst open with a loud noise. Virginia stepped onto the landing, very pale, carrying a small box. Everyone rushed up to her. Mrs. Otis held her tightly in her arms, the Duke covered her with passionate kisses, and the twins danced wildly around them.

“Good heavens, child! Where have you been?” Mr. Otis asked, sounding rather angry because he thought she had been playing a foolish trick. “Cecil and I have ridden all over the countryside looking for you, and your mother has been terrified. You must never play another practical joke like this.”

“Except on the Ghost! Except on the Ghost!” the twins shouted, leaping about.

“My darling, thank God we’ve found you. You must never leave my side again,” Mrs. Otis murmured. She kissed the trembling girl and smoothed her tangled golden hair.

“Papa,” Virginia said quietly, “I have been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He had been very wicked, but he was truly sorry for everything he had done. Before he died, he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.”

The family stared at her, speechless with amazement. But she looked entirely solemn and serious. Turning, she led them through the opening in the wooden wall panels and down a narrow secret passage. Washington followed with a burning candle he had picked up from the table. At last they reached a large oak door covered with rusty nails. Virginia touched it, and it swung open on its heavy hinges. They entered a small, low room with an arched ceiling and one tiny window covered by bars. A huge iron ring was fixed into the wall. Chained to it was a thin skeleton, stretched full length on the stone floor. Its long, bare finger bones seemed to be reaching for an old-fashioned plate and jug placed just beyond its grasp. The jug had clearly once held water, for green mold covered its inside. On the plate there was nothing except a heap of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, clasped her small hands, and began to pray without speaking. The others watched in astonishment as the secret of this terrible tragedy lay revealed before them.

He told us that, travelling from his home through Datchet, he had been surprised to see smoke rising from the inn’s chimney. Thinking he might find fellow travellers gathered there, he knocked and was let in. Only Lucy and her mother were in the house. An attack of rheumatism had left her mother unable to use her limbs, and one after another the remaining people in the district had departed, leaving the two women alone. Lucy begged him to stay. In a week or two her mother would improve, and then they could leave; if abandoned in such a helpless and lonely state, they would die. The man explained that his wife and children were already among the emigrants, which, in his view, made it impossible to remain. As a last resort, Lucy entrusted him with a letter for Idris, to be delivered wherever he encountered us. This responsibility, at least, he carried out, and Idris was deeply moved as she received the following letter:

“DEAR LADY,

“I am certain you will remember me and feel for me, and I dare to hope you will help. What other hope do I have? Please forgive the way I write; I am so distressed and confused. A month ago, my dear mother lost the use of her limbs. She is improving already, and I am sure that in another month she could travel with the arrangements you so kindly offered to make for us. But now everyone has gone—everyone. As they left, each person said that perhaps my mother would recover before we were entirely deserted. Three days ago I went to see Samuel Woods, who had stayed behind until the last because of his newborn child. Since his family is large, I hoped to persuade them to wait a little longer for us. Instead, I found their house empty. I had seen no one since then until this kind man arrived. What will become of us? My mother does not know our situation. She is so ill that I have kept it from her.

“Won’t you send someone to help us? I am sure that, left as we are, we will die in misery. If I tried to move my mother now, she would die on the road. And if, once she improves, I somehow managed—I cannot imagine how—to find the right roads and travel all those many, many miles to the sea, you would already be in France. Between us would lie the great ocean, which frightens even sailors.”
